title: Nausea and Vomiting Assessment
summary: A clinician-facing prompt for assessing nausea and vomiting, identifying serious underlying causes, assessing dehydration risk, and supporting safe management and safety-netting.

sections.title: Assessment priorities
sections.intro: Use this guide as a prompt. It does not replace clinical judgement, imaging or urgent escalation when serious pathology is suspected.

items.title: Must confirm or exclude
mustConfirmOrExclude: Dehydration and electrolyte imbalance (dry mucous membranes, reduced urine output, hypotension).
Acute abdomen or surgical emergency (severe pain, peritoneal signs, bowel obstruction).
Meningitis or other CNS infection (fever, neck stiffness, altered consciousness).
Increased intracranial pressure (progressive headache, papilloedema, focal neurological signs).
Myocardial infarction or acute coronary syndrome (chest pain, dyspnoea, ECG changes).
Metabolic emergencies (DKA, hypercalcaemia, renal failure).
Pregnancy or gynaecological emergency (last menstrual period, pelvic pain).
Medication toxicity or overdose (recent drug exposure, altered consciousness).
items.importantLimitation: Vomiting can mask serious pathology. Red-flag features warrant investigation even if vomiting is apparently benign.

sections.title: Focused history
sections.intro: Characterise onset, pattern and associated symptoms to guide diagnosis.

items.title: Nausea and vomiting characteristics
mustConfirmOrExclude: Onset: sudden vs. gradual; duration.
Pattern: morning vs. throughout day; relation to food or movement.
Content: clear, bilious, bloody, coffee-ground (haematemesis)?
Frequency: single episode vs. persistent vomiting.
Associated: abdominal pain, diarrhoea, headache, fever or dizziness?

items.title: Systemic and constitutional features
mustConfirmOrExclude: Fever, rigors or signs of infection.
Headache, photophobia or neck stiffness (meningitis).
Abdominal pain: location, severity, type (sharp, cramping, constant)?
Diarrhoea, constipation or change in bowel habit.
Dizziness, vertigo or balance problems.
Weakness, confusion or altered consciousness.

items.title: Red-flag features in history
mustConfirmOrExclude: Severe abdominal pain or peritoneal signs (acute abdomen).
Bilious or blood-stained vomitus (obstruction or upper GI bleed).
Fever with headache and neck stiffness (meningitis).
Severe persistent vomiting with inability to drink (dehydration risk).
Chest pain or shortness of breath (cardiac, pulmonary).
Vertigo with vomiting (vestibular, CNS).
Altered consciousness or focal neurological signs (CNS pathology).
Recent medication change or overdose history.
Pregnancy or possibility of pregnancy.
Sudden onset severe headache (SAH, meningitis).

sections.title: Serious pathology screen
sections.intro: Positive features should trigger urgent investigation or referral.

items.title: Acute abdomen or surgical emergency
urgentFeatures: Severe abdominal pain with peritoneal signs (guarding, rebound).
Bilious vomiting with abdominal distension (obstruction).
Bloody vomitus (upper GI bleed) or coffee-ground appearance.
Severe pain localised to right lower quadrant (appendicitis).
Recent surgery or abdominal trauma.
implications: Urgent hospital assessment; abdominal imaging required.

items.title: Meningitis or sepsis
urgentFeatures: Fever with headache, neck stiffness and vomiting.
Altered consciousness or rash.
Fever with severe systemic illness or signs of shock.
implications: Emergency referral and empiric antibiotics if meningitis suspected.

items.title: Increased intracranial pressure
urgentFeatures: Progressive headache with vomiting.
Projectile vomiting (without nausea).
Morning vomiting, drowsiness or cognitive changes.
Papilloedema or focal neurological signs.

items.title: Metabolic emergency
urgentFeatures: Known diabetes with vomiting and altered consciousness (DKA).
Severe vomiting with severe hypercalcaemia signs (weakness, confusion).
Renal failure with vomiting and electrolyte disturbance.
implications: Hospital assessment; blood tests and IV fluids required.

sections.title: Focused examination
sections.intro: Assess for dehydration, peritoneal signs and systemic illness.

items.title: Dehydration assessment
howToTest: Mucous membranes: moist, dry or very dry.
Vital signs: heart rate, blood pressure (postural if possible).
Ability to drink and retain fluids.
normal: Moist mucous membranes, normal turgor, normal vital signs.
abnormal: Dry mucous membranes, reduced turgor, tachycardia, hypotension, reduced urine.
implications: Assess dehydration severity; IV fluids likely needed if moderate/severe.

items.title: Abdominal examination
howToTest: Palpate: tenderness (diffuse vs. localised), guarding, rebound, masses.
abnormal: Peritoneal signs, distension, absent bowel sounds, focal tenderness.
implications: Peritoneal signs suggest surgical pathology; absent sounds suggest obstruction.

items.title: Neurological and meningeal assessment
howToTest: Meningeal signs: neck stiffness, Kernig and Brudzinski signs.
Focal neurological signs: pupils, eye movements, motor and sensory.
normal: Alert, no neck stiffness, no focal signs.
abnormal: Altered consciousness, neck stiffness, focal neurological signs.
implications: Neurological signs suggest CNS pathology; meningeal signs require emergency referral.

sections.title: Common clinical patterns
sections.intro: Pattern recognition supports diagnosis and management decisions.

items.title: Viral gastroenteritis
commonFindings: Sudden onset nausea and vomiting, often with diarrhoea.
Preceding viral illness or sick contact.
Mild dehydration without severe systemic illness.
implications: Supportive care with oral rehydration; no antibiotics.

items.title: Medication-related nausea and vomiting
commonFindings: Temporal relationship to new medication or dose change.
Opioids, antibiotics, NSAIDs, chemotherapy most common.
Improves with medication change or dose adjustment.
implications: Review medications; consider alternatives or antiemetics.

items.title: Migraine-associated nausea and vomiting
commonFindings: Headache with nausea and vomiting (often disabling).
implications: Treat migraine; antiemetics and abortive therapy as needed.

items.title: Pregnancy-related nausea (hyperemesis)
commonFindings: Hyperemesis gravidarum: severe persistent vomiting with weight loss and dehydration.
implications: Mild: reassurance and dietary advice. Severe: hospital admission for IV fluids and antiemetics.

sections.title: Management and disposition
sections.intro: Base decisions on serious pathology assessment and dehydration severity.

items.title: Rehydration
mustConfirmOrExclude: Mild dehydration: oral rehydration solution, small frequent amounts.
Moderate dehydration: IV fluids if unable to tolerate oral.
Severe dehydration: hospital admission for IV fluids and monitoring.

items.title: Community management is appropriate when
mustConfirmOrExclude: No red-flag features present.
No peritoneal signs.
Mild to moderate dehydration only.
Likely viral gastroenteritis or medication-related nausea.
Able to tolerate oral intake.

items.title: Urgent hospital referral
urgentFeatures: Severe abdominal pain with peritoneal signs.
Fever with headache and meningeal signs.
Bloody or coffee-ground vomitus.
Severe persistent vomiting with inability to drink.
Altered consciousness or focal neurological signs.
Signs of shock or severe dehydration.

items.title: Nausea and vomiting
safetyNetting: Call 999 or go to ED immediately for: severe abdominal pain with vomiting; vomiting blood or coffee-ground material; fever with severe headache and neck stiffness; altered consciousness; severe dizziness; or signs of shock.

Contact your GP or go to ED same-day for: persistent vomiting preventing fluid intake; severe abdominal pain; blood in vomitus; high fever (>38.5°C); unable to keep fluids down for more than a few hours; or signs of dehydration (dark urine, extreme thirst).
Speak to your GP if: nausea and vomiting persist beyond 2-3 days; you are unable to tolerate food or fluids; you want antiemetic advice; or you want to discuss medication-related symptoms.
